# Preface {.unnumbered}

`fast.string` is an R package for the string, date and name-matching work
that record linkage and ETL pipelines spend their time on. It has three
layers:

- **`rLink()`**, which links or deduplicates data frames in one call:
  multi-pass blocking, any number of comparators, one table of scored
  candidate pairs (@sec-uc-link).
- **The record-linkage primitives base R does not have** — phonetic
  blocking keys (Soundex, NYSIIS, Double Metaphone, Daitch-Mokotoff,
  Caverphone, ...), string similarities and edit distances (Jaro-Winkler,
  Levenshtein, Editex, q-gram overlap, the RapidFuzz scorers), candidate
  search without a comparison matrix, and connected-component clustering.
- **Faster equivalents of the everyday functions** — `grepl()`,
  `grep()`, `sub()`, `gsub()`, `trimws()`, `substr()`, `nchar()`,
  `chartr()`, `strsplit()`, `toupper()`, date parsing and formatting —
  so the cleaning either side of a linkage is not the slow part.

Large workloads are parallelised via Intel TBB (through
[RcppParallel](https://rcppcore.github.io/RcppParallel/)), with
[PCRE2](https://www.pcre.org/) doing the regex work and
a prepared byte-oriented searcher handling fixed/literal matching.
Performance depends on string length, match density, value reuse, matrix
shape, and available cores. Some operations (parallel Jaro-Winkler,
multi-pattern substitution in one pass) have no base R equivalent at all.

## Why this exists

Record linkage and data-cleaning pipelines spend a surprising fraction of
their wall-clock time in string operations that look trivial in isolation —
`trimws()` on a column, a `gsub()` to strip punctuation, `grepl()` to flag a
pattern — but get called over and over on multi-million-row name/address
files. Individually each call is fast; in aggregate, on a 5M-row file, they
add up to minutes of CPU time spent doing work a single core could be doing
across eight or sixteen instead.

Four things are conspicuously *not* one function each in base R, despite
being everywhere in this kind of pipeline:

- **Phonetic blocking keys** (Soundex, NYSIIS, Refined Soundex, Cologne,
  Double Metaphone, Caverphone) — used to group *probably-same* names
  before running an expensive pairwise comparison within each group, rather
  than comparing every record against every other record.
- **Fuzzy string similarity** (Jaro-Winkler, edit distance, q-gram
  overlap) — base R has no notion of "how similar are these two strings,"
  only exact (`==`) or pattern (`grepl()`) matching.
- **Multi-token name comparison** — `"Kyle John Haynes"` and
  `"John Kylie Haynes"` are obviously the same person with two tokens
  swapped, but a plain character-by-character comparison scores that badly.
- **Per-element match counting** — `grepl()` answers "is there a match";
  counting how *many* means `gregexpr()` plus a `vapply()` that allocates a
  position vector per row only to take its length.

`fast.string` exists to make all of the above fast enough to run
unblinkingly on real-sized data, and to package the boring-but-essential
80% (trimming, substitution, date parsing) so a project doesn't need five
different dependencies for five different speed problems.

## How it fits with record-linkage packages

`rLink()` covers one step of a linkage: two files in, scored candidate
pairs out. It does not classify them. Estimating match probabilities from
the scores — EM-fitted Fellegi-Sunter weights, training against a
labelled sample — is what
[`RecordLinkage`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=RecordLinkage),
[`reclin2`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=reclin2) and
[`fastLink`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=fastLink) are for, and
they do it well. The natural division is `rLink()` for the blocking and
the per-field comparison, where the string work and the parallelism are,
and one of those packages for the model that decides. @sec-benchmarks
compares this package's comparison primitives directly against the
equivalent functions in `RecordLinkage` and `stringdist` at scale, and
@sec-wf-score shows how far hand weights get you and where they stop.

## How this book is organised

- **Getting started** — what `fast.string` is for and how it's positioned
  against base R, `stringi`/`stringr`, `stringdist`, and `RecordLinkage`
  (@sec-about), then a hands-on tour of every function group
  (@sec-quickstart).
- **Use cases** — task-oriented recipes: cleaning and standardising text
  (entities, accents, abbreviation dictionaries, leading zeros, spelling
  variants; @sec-uc-clean), finding, flagging and extracting values from
  free text (@sec-uc-extract), profiling and validating columns (format
  shapes, identifier check digits; @sec-uc-profile), matching, deduplicating
  and linking records at scale with `rLink()` and the primitives under it
  (@sec-uc-link), and pseudonymising
  identifiers with keyed hashes (@sec-uc-privacy).
- **Under the hood** — the algorithms (@sec-theory): how regex and
  fixed-literal matching differ, how the bit-parallel Jaro-Winkler
  implementation works, how the phonetic schemes trade block size against
  recall, and how multi-token name comparison resolves reordered tokens —
  followed by a full worked record-linkage pipeline (@sec-workflow) that
  links two files of people whose names, dates of birth, addresses, sex and
  postcodes are each recorded differently: profiling, standardising field
  by field, multi-pass blocking, per-field scoring, a defensible
  accept/review/reject decision, entity identifiers, and a measurement of
  how well it worked against a known truth.
- **Reference** — an exhaustive per-function reference with every
  argument and runnable examples (@sec-reference); the heavy benchmark
  chapter at **3 million strings**, with `base`, `stringi`, `stringdist`,
  and `RecordLinkage` as comparison baselines (@sec-benchmarks); and a
  troubleshooting/FAQ chapter (@sec-troubleshooting).

## A quick taste

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_setup.R")
```

A whole linkage — blocking, scoring, one row per candidate pair — is
one call. Two small files of people, with a surname spelled two ways, a
nickname instead of a registered given name, and a date of birth whose day
and month were transposed:

```{r}
#| label: teaser-rlink
enrol <- data.frame(
    id      = c("E1", "E2", "E3", "E4"),
    given   = c("ROBERT", "ELIZABETH", "MOHAMMED", "LI"),
    surname = c("O'BRIEN", "SMITH-JONES", "EL-MASRI", "NGUYEN"),
    dob     = as.Date(c("1985-03-05", "1972-11-30", "1990-07-14", "1964-02-29")),
    sex     = c("M", "F", "M", "F"))

claims <- data.frame(
    id      = c("C1", "C2", "C3"),
    given   = c("BOB", "LIZ", "MOHAMED"),
    surname = c("OBRIEN", "SMITH JONES", "EL MASRI"),
    dob     = as.Date(c("1985-05-03", "1972-11-30", "1990-07-14")),
    sex     = c("M", "F", "M"))

rLink(enrol, claims,
      block   = list(exact_dob    = list(dob),
                     surname_year = list(soundex(surname),
                                         format_date(dob, "y"))),
      compare = list(sn  = jaro_winkler_tokens(surname),
                     gn  = jaro_winkler(given),
                     dob = (function(a, b) as.numeric(a == b))(dob)),
      keep    = c("id", "given", "surname", "dob"))
```

All three claims found their person, and the `pass` column says how: two
on the exact date of birth, and Robert O'Brien — whose day and month had
been swapped — on the second pass, a phonetic surname code plus the year
alone. `jaro_winkler_tokens()` scores
`"SMITH-JONES"` against `"SMITH JONES"` at 1, because it folds punctuation
and word order inside the comparison. @sec-uc-link and @sec-workflow take
this all the way through on data that is properly messy.

And the ordinary string work underneath it, on a million values:

```{r}
#| label: teaser-speed
n <- 1e6
nm  <- sprintf("%s %s", sample(c("John", "Mary", "Kyle", "Priya"), n, TRUE),
               sample(c("Smith", "O'Brien", "Haynes", "Nguyen"), n, TRUE))
dob <- as.Date("1950-01-01") + sample(0:25000, n, TRUE)

rbind(toupper     = system.time(toupper(nm))[1:3],
      fupper      = system.time(fupper(nm))[1:3],
      format      = system.time(format(dob, "%Y-%m-%d"))[1:3],
      format_date = system.time(format_date(dob))[1:3])
```

`format_date()` is the extreme case: `format()` on a `Date` reaches
`strftime()` once per element, and replacing that with integer calendar
arithmetic is worth two orders of magnitude. Most functions here are
nearer 2—10x, a few are no faster than base R at all
(@sec-troubleshooting says which), and the phonetic codes and similarity
scores have no base R equivalent to be compared with.
